national.summary: The MV Odyssey had been on an around-the-world cruise when it suspended its planned three-year voyage due to the sharp rise in fuel costs.
national.body: A U.S. cruise ship that forced all its passengers to disembark in Cambodia after suspending its operations last week has departed the Southeast Asian nation with only crew aboard, Cambodian officials said Wednesday. The MV Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, had been on an around-the-world cruise when it suspended its planned three-year voyage due to the sharp rise in fuel costs. It had been docked for a scheduled stop at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, when on Oct. 28 its 203 passengers were suddenly told they had to disembark within a few hours.The ship left Sihanoukville late Tuesday with only crew and other personnel on board, said Tang Sochetkresna, director of the Tourism Department of Preah Sihanouk province. He said he didn't know the ship's next destination, but multiple sources familiar with the matter previously told CBS News the ship will be moved to Singapore, where it could eventually be auctioned off. The cruise ship is now under control of its lender, according to a message sent to residents and obtained by CBS News. Company leadership, however, said they're optimistic they can get the ship back — if they find an operational partner. "This is a 30- to 90-day process, and, during that process, we have time to get a restructure done," Mike Petterson, the company's founder and executive chairman, told CBS News.Sochetkresna said that nearly 100 passengers remained in Sihanoukville, while others were visiting other parts of Cambodia or had traveled on to other countries. Most of the ship's passengers were Americans. The ship, with its 650-passenger capacity, had 156 crew members on board, but it was not clear how many departed with the ship. There has been no official announcement of future plans for the cruise ship. Media reports suggested that a creditor had taken over its management and was having it sailed to Singapore, Southeast Asia's main maritime hub. The abrupt end to the ship's voyage has drawn widespread attention because it had touted itself as a floating home, combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Several passengers said they had paid more than $300,000 for a suite for the lifetime of the vessel. national.title: ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline
national.summary: As South Africans vote in local elections, residents tell the BBC they are tired of the poor quality of services they get.
national.body:
South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's biggest party, the African National Congress (ANC).

This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes.

Election officials say voting is going smoothly, despite long queues at some polling stations.

Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.

For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.

Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.

At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.

Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral.

national.title: Rwanda's army team removed from Africa league after US sanctions, NBA says
national.summary: The US imposed sanctions on Rwanda's army over its role in the conflict in DR Congo.
national.body:
The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.

The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).

However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.

The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March.

The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".

Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.

Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.

national.title: Key moments from a night of midterm election firsts
national.summary: Democrats have taken control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency - proving moments of celebration.
national.body:
Democrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.

Projected results have provided the party with a number of things to celebrate - and rival Republicans some reasons to commiserate.

These are some of the key moments so far, which include a number of historic firsts.

Democrats have tallied up victories in states that were comfortably won by Trump two years ago, registering sizeable swings in the likes of Texas, Kansas, Ohio and South Carolina.

Among the senior party figures who have cheered the results are Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the Speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.

"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.

If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next Speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Johnson and becoming the first black person to fill that role.

national.title: Review: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is superb, streamlined and safe
national.summary: Nintendo's new Ocarina of Time remake enshrines its place in the gaming canon for generations to come. But despite its stupendous production values, the game left me feeling oddly bereft.
national.body:
Link, the Hero of Time, grown-up and newly awoken from a magical seven-year slumber. Nintendo hide caption

With its tale of an idyllic world despoiled by the lust for power, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time feels as relevant today as it did in 1998. Nintendo's new remake, out Thursday on the Switch 2, enshrines its place in the gaming canon for generations to come. But despite its stupendous production values and painstaking details, the game left me feeling oddly bereft.

Perhaps I should have expected as much. Ocarina of Time weaponizes nostalgia even within its narrative, as the protagonist Link ventures to save his post-apocalyptic world as an adult after first working through it as a kid. You'll uncover old characters enduring new catastrophes. You'll try to rescue everyone you meet. You'll strive to bring things back to how they were before — no, better than they were before.

Seven years stretch between Link's childhood and adult adventures. 28 years yawn between the remake and the original's release. Both in and out of the game, Ocarina of Time makes us yearn for an idealized past.

Decent remakes evoke how you remember a game rather than re-create dated controls and chunky graphics. In myriad small ways, Nintendo has brought Ocarina of Time up to contemporary standards while (mostly) preserving its soul.

In one of the game's most poignant scenes, kid Link answers to the call to adventure, leaving his friend Saria and the Kokiri Forest they called home. Nintendo hide caption

I miss the thoughtfully-composed camera angles from the original, but quickly got used to the over-the-shoulder camera the remake employs (though I was irked that it abandoned the top-down view when you sneak into Hyrule Castle). The new jump and sprint buttons made navigating the world feel more natural. Combat's smoother too, though it's still not easy to switch between targeted enemies (unlike modern third-person games like Elden Ring , where you can toggle between foes by simply flicking the right stick).

You can, thankfully, swap between items in a quick menu — the same system introduced to the series in 2023's Tears of the Kingdom and continued in 2024's Echoes of Wisdom . It's still not as fast as I'd wish (I'd have preferred a customizable wheel), but I vastly prefer it to constantly pausing to access my equipment. It made it easy to change my strategy on the fly. I'd often cast Naryu's Love and deploy Bombchus, for example, where before I'd mostly stick to the Longshot and Bow.

national.summary: The 29-year-old democratic socialist from Colorado made history as the first woman from Generation Z to be elected to Congress.
national.body: Washington — Melat Kiros, who defeated Democratic Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado's primary in July, was born in 1997, the same year DeGette began her decadeslong congressional career.On Tuesday night, the 29-year-old democratic socialist made history as the first Generation Z woman to be elected to Congress. national.title: US contractor gave Ethiopia secrets to help kill Tigray fighters
national.summary: The Ethiopian-born American citizen admitted sharing dozens of classified documents with senior Ethiopian officials.
national.body:
An Ethiopian-born American citizen has pleaded guilty to passing highly classified intelligence to Ethiopia, including information he hoped would help target and kill fighters from the Tigray region during the country's 2020-22 civil war.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, a former US contractor, admitted sharing dozens of classified documents and photographs with senior Ethiopian officials over more than two years, the US Department of Justice said.

"In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security," said US Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

The 54-year-old faces up to 22 years in prison under a plea agreement.

Abraham had worked as a contractor at the State Department, Justice Department and National Reconnaissance Office, the agency responsible for US intelligence satellites.

Prosecutors said Abraham worked with senior figures in Ethiopia's political, military and intelligence establishments between 2021 and his arrest in August 2023.

He secretly removed classified material from secure government facilities, sometimes copying sensitive information into handwritten notes that he carried out of the buildings. He used his position as an IT administrator to extract electronic intelligence files.

"Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia," prosecutors said.

national.title: Trump takes aim at Republicans but says Democrats did a 'good job'
national.summary: He wrote on Truth Social that Republicans would have won "in a landslide" if his name had been on the ballot.
national.body:
US President Donald Trump has taken aim at Republicans and conceded that the Democrats have done "a good job" in the US midterm elections, as they take control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in a momentous win.

In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump derided Greg Abbott, who lost the Texas governor race to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, saying Abbott wouldn't have lost if he "hadn't become a RINO in the last six months", using the acronym for "Republican in Name Only".

The president said that if he had been on the ballot, the Republicans "would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

But he also said that he accepted the results of the election, telling The New York Times that he was "absolutely willing to accept" them.

While speaking to the paper, Trump added that he would "look forward to working with" the Democrats.

In a separate interview with Fox News, he said he was "a little surprised" at the outcome. "I thought they'd do better," he said, referring to the Republican candidates.

"The Democrats did a good job. they fought hard," he told the network.

But he added that the Democrats would send "insane" legislation to his desk that he would veto.

national.title: Iran's chief negotiator says Americans voted 'no to war'
national.summary: "We endorse this message," Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf says, as Donald Trump acknowledges the conflict's role in the Republican Party's defeat.
national.body:
Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the US has said that Americans have "said NO TO WAR", after President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered a stunning defeat in the midterm elections.

"We endorse this message," parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X.

"If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," he warned.

Trump acknowledged on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in petrol prices. But he insisted that he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran in February.

In an interview with Fox News, Trump said of the midterm results: "I think a part of it was Iran".

He went on to say: "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that."

Speaking separately to the BBC's US news partner, CBS News, Trump said the conflict would end "when I say it ends".

In recent weeks, the president has warned that the US and Israel could return to all-out war after the midterms if a deal to end the conflict cannot be reached with Iran.

national.title: Democrat Rosenthal wins ugly race for Texas railroad commissioner
national.summary: Republican Bo French attracted attention when he posted a photo of students of South Asian descent cheering at a football game with a caption saying the University of Texas has a "problem" that is "far worse than anyone imagined."
national.body: Democrat Jon Rosenthal won the Texas Railroad Commissioner race, CBS News projects, defeating Republican Bo French after the GOP candidate refused to reconsider his racist, anti-Muslim and antisemitic comments.With about 93% of votes counted, Rosenthal led French 52.5% to 45.6%.The powerful Texas railroad commissioner does not deal with railroads, but instead regulates the state's oil and gas industry, which accounts for over 40% of the U.S. crude oil output. There are three total commissioners â the other two are Republicans.Rosenthal is currently a state representative from Houston and a former oil field engineer, who worked in the industry for 25 years. French originally hails from Midland and had been the Tarrant County Republican chairman. Although Rosenthal and French have differences on oil and gas policy, the main issues in the race had come down to French's controversial comments about immigrants, Muslims and Jews in what was already shaping up to be a difficult year for Texas Republicans. Ahead of the May runoff, many of Texas' prominent elected Republicans united against French's candidacy, although he ultimately won the nomination. In September, French made national headlines when he posted that University of Texas students were a "problem" because the students appeared to be of South Asian descent. In another post with the same photo, French said, "Like body-cams exposed criminals, social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners." Several of the students came forward later and said they were American citizens. Shortly after his post, Republican Sen. John Cornyn, who earlier lost his primary against Ken Paxton, said he would not be voting for French. Other Texas Republicans, including Karl Rove, said they would not be voting for French. French still raised more than $700,000 after the social media post about the UT students. Rosenthal had brought in more than $500,000 in the same time period. Even ahead of his primary win, French had previously posted antisemitic and anti-Muslim comments and had said in his campaign platform that he wanted to root out DEI policies, "stop the Islamic invasion of Texas" and "support life and the nuclear family."The last time a Democrat won a race for railroad commissioner was 1990.

national.title: Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House
national.summary: As speaker, the New York Democrat would be second in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president. He has vowed to focus on affordability and holding the administration accountable.
national.body:
After helping to deliver a decisive victory for House Democrats in the midterm elections, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., appears all but certain to become the first Black lawmaker to be elected speaker of the House.

Jeffries was elected House minority leader in 2022 and is the first Black politician to lead either party in the House or Senate. As speaker, Jeffries would be second in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president.

His elevation to speaker would represent the pinnacle of a nearly 14-year House tenure, a span that has seen Jeffries rise from a rank-and-file member focused on criminal justice policy to a top party lieutenant under former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then minority leader.

It's a rise that has meant securing buy-in from a diverse and often fractious House Democratic caucus — a task that may prove only more challenging as the Democratic Party now looks to make good on its promises to voters.

"This is a change election, and we understand as House Democrats that we need to deliver dramatic change," Jeffries said on Tuesday night. "Things are broken. We need a Congress that puts the American people first."

Born and raised in Brooklyn, N.Y., Jeffries has represented parts of the borough in Congress since 2013 and served as a leader in both the influential Congressional Black Caucus and the House Democratic caucus.

Before entering politics, Jeffries served as a lawyer in private practice and credits his time helping members of his community through a law school legal clinic as sparking his interest in criminal justice reform.

"I think over time it did inform that if I had the opportunity to go into the practice of law, or eventually public service, that I wanted to do something about the broken criminal justice system," Jeffries said in a 2023 interview with NY1.

national.title: These 9 candidates for governor just made history
national.summary: Voters on Tuesday elected the nation's first Black woman governor and the nation's first Native American woman governor.
national.body:
Voters in nine states made history on Tuesday with their choices for governor.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, who won her race to be Georgia's next governor, will be the country's first Black woman elected governor of any state. The 56-year-old served as mayor of Atlanta from 2018-2022, then served as an adviser to former President Joe Biden. Her defeat of Republican billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson makes Lance Bottoms the first Democrat to win a governor's race in the state in more than two decades.

New Mexico's Deb Haaland, who is of Pueblo Indian descent , will be the first Native American woman governor. The Democrat, who defeated Republican Gregg Hull, served in Congress before becoming Interior secretary under Biden. She made history in each of those roles, too — as one of the first Native American women elected to Congress and the first Native American cabinet secretary.

Democrat Xavier Becerra will be the first elected Latino governor of California when he takes office, while Democrat Gina Hinojosa will be the first Latina governor of Texas . Becerra, a former California attorney general and former member of Congress who served as U.S. secretary of Health and Human Services in the Biden administration, will succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom after handily defeating Republican Steve Hilton, a political outsider.

Hinojosa, a Texas state representative, defeated incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, one the country's most influential governors and an ally of President Trump. Hinojosa's win follows a demographic shift in the state, which has seen a surge in its Latino population. Hinojosa will be Texas' first Democratic governor in more than 30 years.

Voters in Florida and Wisconsin elected the first Black governors in their states — Republican Byron Donalds in the Sunshine State and Democrat David Crowley in the Badger State .

President Donald Trump listens as Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, speaks at a campaign rally in Daytona Beach, Fla., Friday. Donalds won his election and is set to become Florida's first Black governor. Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo hide caption

Donalds, who had the backing of President Trump and a hefty election war chest, beat Democrat David Jolly by campaigning on affordability and promising to continue the conservative politics of outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis. Donalds has been in Congress since 2021 and served two terms in the state legislature.

national.title: How America voted in maps and charts
national.summary: See the maps and charts that show how America voted in the US midterm elections.
national.body:
It's been an extraordinary night for the Democrats in the US midterms.

They have taken control of the Senate and the House of Representatives too.

The results in the Senate are beyond what the Democrats would have expected. North Carolina was a likely pick-up but South Carolina was a huge shock and Kansas had not returned a Democratic senator since 1932.

national.title: Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford beats GOP incumbent for governor
national.summary: Democrat Aaron Ford defeated Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. He's set to become Nevada's first Black governor.
national.body:
RENO, Nev. – In what was considered one of the most competitive gubernatorial races in the U.S. , Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford unseated Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, according to an Associated Press race call.

The Democrat will be the first Black governor of a state west of the Mississippi River . He was previously Nevada's first Black Senate majority leader and attorney general. He was first elected to the state legislature in 2012, and before that practiced law privately and taught math .

As attorney general, Ford successfully joined lawsuits against the Trump administration to uphold birthright citizenship , stop federal election interference , and restore education funding.

Lombardo was elected in 2022 and was a sheriff before that. He was endorsed by President Trump.

Throughout his campaign, Ford blamed the state's economic woes on Lombardo and Trump, including some of the highest gas prices in the country at over $5 per gallon and declining tourism , which is one of the main sources of revenue, due to tariffs and immigration crackdowns.

Nevada also risks losing an estimated $1.2 billion in federal funding due to changes to Medicaid, food assistance and cuts in the Affordable Care Act health insurance.

Ford has pledged to bring back bills outgoing Lombardo killed in his record-breaking vetoes , including limiting the number of homes large corporations can buy and giving the state the power to adopt Medicaid negotiated prescription drug prices .

Lombardo campaigned on telling voters he would continue the work he did in the first term when he increased pay for teachers and state employees and set aside $133 million to develop housing for middle-income Nevadans.

national.body: Washington — GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection in the Nebraska Senate race, CBS News projects, fending off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn. Ricketts, 62, is a former Nebraska governor who was appointed to the Senate in 2023. He faced off against Osborn, a former union leader who was making his second Senate bid. Osborn, 51, lost in 2024 to Republican Sen. Deb Fischer by seven points. And with Democrats again clearing the way for him this cycle, he made a play to oust Ricketts in the conservative state. Nebraskans haven't elected a candidate who wasn't a Republican since 2006. But with a large share of nonpartisan voters and an unfavorable environment for the GOP amid the unpopular war with Iran and high gas and diesel prices, the race proved to be competitive. Though Osborn has said he wouldn't have caucused with Democrats, Ricketts' projected victory wards off an outcome that could have subtracted further from their majority. national.title: Delhi air quality worsens ahead of Diwali as firework restrictions enter force
national.summary: On Wednesday morning, Delhi's air quality index reading stood at 377, in the "very poor" category.
national.body:
Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.

The city's air quality index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.

Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.

Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.

GRAP is a set of emergency measures that become progressively stricter as pollution levels rise. The latest restrictions include more intensive road cleaning, higher parking charges to discourage private vehicle use and increased public transport services. Delhi Metro has introduced 20 additional weekday train trips, while authorities have been directed to stagger government office timings to ease traffic congestion.

Officials said the measures were introduced after forecasts suggested air quality would remain very poor over the coming days.

Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.

The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.

national.summary: The raced heated up in its final weeks after the Republican contender released an ad featuring Acton's mother.
national.body:
Democrat Amy Acton has defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to win the Ohio governorship in a bitterly contested race.

With the projected victory, Acton becomes the first Democrat and the first ever woman to win the Ohio governor's race in two decades.

Ohio, a key battleground for much of the 2000s, has voted for Republican Donald Trump in the last three presidential elections, including by 11 points in 2024.

But the gubernatorial race, where voter frustration over the economy and the cost of living was the central theme, took an unexpected turn after the Ramaswamy campaign released a deeply personal attack ad featuring Acton's estranged mother.

In the ad, Acton's mother Donna Arthur said her daughter "lied her entire life". It did not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child.

The controversial advert loomed over the last weeks of the race. It was criticised by former South Carolina Governor Republican Nikki Haley, while Ohio's current Republican Governor Mike DeWine called it "deeply troubling".

However, some defended it, including President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance.

Trump described it as "powerful" and encouraged Ramaswamy to keep it running, while Vance, the state's former senator, said he would like fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about the ad and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party.

national.summary: Maine's Senate race was mired in controversy after Democratic nominee Graham Planter withdrew following multiple scandals.
national.body:
Democrat Troy Jackson has defeated longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins in Maine, unseating the famous moderate senator in a race marked by controversy.

Jackson entered the race after replacing Graham Platner, the Democratic nominee who withdrew following a series of scandals.

First elected in 1996, Collins was the only Republican senator representing a state that has consistently voted Democratic in presidential elections since 1992.

She has cultivated a reputation as a moderate and sought to distance herself from President Donald Trump during her campaign. Jackson, a former logger, campaigned on workers' rights and accused Collins of yielding to pressure from the president.

TOP MOMENTS: Ecstatic scenes and historic moments: What's happened so far in the midterms

Collins and Jackson went head to head during state debates, with Jackson making national headlines when he told the 73-year-old to "shut up".

He entered the campaign late in the season, after Planter withdrew following a series of controversies, including allegations of sexual assault. Platner has denied the allegations.

Jackson had failed to win the Democratic gubernatorial primary, but won the senate nomination in a special convention. He positioned himself as a working-class candidate and backed progressive policies like abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

national.title: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeats Republican Mike Rogers in key Michigan Senate race
national.summary: El-Sayed's campaign tested how an antiestablishment candidate on the left would fare in a perennial Midwest battleground. With the win, he'll become the first Muslim American to serve in the Senate.
national.body:
DETROIT — Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won the U.S. Senate election in Michigan, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

One of the most closely watched elections in the U.S., the race in Michigan tested how an antiestablishment candidate on the left would fare in a perennial Midwest battleground.

El-Sayed will be the first Muslim American to serve in the Senate.

The 42-year-old former public health official defeated former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers. Rogers lost his first bid for the Senate in 2024.

Harnessing anger over the cost of living and corruption, El-Sayed galvanized young and infrequent voters by focusing on passing single-payer healthcare and curbing the influence of corporate money in politics.

He is not a democratic socialist, unlike several candidates whose insurgent campaigns gained traction in primaries this cycle, though his campaign was backed by some of the biggest stars on the political left.

His positions on Israel alienated some Jewish voters, including comments after a truck-ramming attack at a synagogue preschool in metro Detroit — for which he later offered an apology — and campaigning during the primary with controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker.

Those were among the dynamics during a heated primary contest that turned into a stand-in for many of the broader debates fueling the direction of the Democratic Party after two years in the political wilderness.

local.title: A big night for Democrats
local.summary: At the local, state, and national level, Democrats made major victories, flipping seats and incumbents handily defeating challengers.
local.body:
Monroe County Democratic candidates won big Tuesday evening, mirroring a national trend and signaling the local Republican party's dwindling influence.

According to unofficial election night results, all incumbent Democratic candidates for local state Senate and Assembly seats, as well as Congressman Joe Morelle, handily won reelection against their Republican challengers. Gov. Kathy Hochul secured a second term in office after facing a challenge from Republican Bruce Blakeman. Meanwhile, Democrats flipped several key local seats long held by Republicans.

At the national level, Democrats appeared poised to take control of both the House of Representatives and Senate, in what appears to be a rebuke of President Donald Trump's policies in his second term in office.

"It's a historic night," Morelle said. "Americans showed up, and I think they had to make a decision on the direction of this government and the direction of this country. They spoke loudly, they spoke clearly, in an overwhelming way, rejected the politics of hatred and divisiveness and corruption. And I couldn't be prouder."

Morelle said his key focuses will be putting an end to stock trading for Congressmembers and Supreme Court Justices and attempting to quell the influence of "dark money" in the House.

Attendees at the celebration party for Monroe County Democrats at the Hyatt Regency in Rochester saw a chance for change.

"One thing I hope, really hope, is that Democrats and Republicans can come together and make good decisions," said Janis White, a party supporter. "...Just come together and make good decisions for the United States."

Some Democrats scored major upsets for seats that have historically been held tightly by the GOP. Republican Gates Town Supervisor Cosmo Giunta, first elected in 2018, lost to Democrat Nick Coffee, who appears to be the first Democrat elected to lead Gates in the town's history.

local.body:
The Fredonia Shakespeare Club welcomed Elizabeth Cady Stanton back at the home of Mary Croxton during its recent meeting.

The Fredonia Censor first recorded Elizabeth Cady Stanton's visit on April 27, 1870. Mrs. Elizabeth C. Stanton (the name she used instead of Mrs. Henry Stanton) was on a Lyceum tour around the country.

The Censor wrote: "The beautiful weather of Saturday, April 23 made it pleasant for an attendance from the surrounding towns, and consequence was a house full of auditors to greet the great advocate of the cause of her sex. Not one was disappointed." The name of the lecture was "Open the Door." ... The argument of the lecture was strong and varied with flashes of wit, pathos and eloquence that retained the unwearied attention of the audience till the close of the two hours...most were unable to deny the brilliancy of the effort as a literary production."

Stanton gave this advice to the girls; "not to marry till they are twenty-five, for they are not fully developed mentally or physically till then. "Women must learn to depend upon themselves. Irving's picture of a stately oak, covered with a clinging vine...when the lightning strikes the oak, or the woodman's axe levels it to the ground, the vine dies with it and there the simile ends. Many a family's dependence is thus stricken down, leaving the mother with not only herself, but a half a dozen children to look out for, and the speaker exhorted the young girls to prepare themselves for such emergencies, instead of expecting and making themselves fit for nothing but "to twine."

E.C. Stanton gave a capital plea, for allowing women on juries, and gave a scathing denunciation of the abominable proceedings allowed in courts when women are on trial, also a review of the old laws of 1848 in reference to the rights of women to their own property and children. She advised the women not to pay taxes till they could have representatives. She went on claiming that the old text of "Wives, obey your Husbands," was of no more authority now than "Honor the King."

She proclaimed that women's suffrage is the paramount issue at present, just as she did in July 1848 at the first Women's Rights Convention in Seneca Falls, New York. Her Declaration of Sentiments: We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights, that among these are life, liberty, and pursuit of happiness; that to secure these rights governments are instituted, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed."

local.title: The rut Is coming: best days for deer hunters
local.summary: As November arrives, deer hunters across Chautauqua County and Western New York are entering one of the most anticipated stretches of the whitetail season. The woods are changing, the days are growing shorter and the excitement is building. The best part of deer season may be just around the corner.
local.body:
As November arrives, deer hunters across Chautauqua County and Western New York are entering one of the most anticipated stretches of the whitetail season. The woods are changing, the days are growing shorter and the excitement is building. The best part of deer season may be just around the corner.

The annual whitetail rut, when bucks focus much of their attention on finding receptive does, can turn an ordinary day in the woods into an unforgettable hunt. During the chase phase, bucks begin searching for does that have not yet entered estrus. They travel more widely, follow fresh scent trails and sometimes appear in places where hunters have seen little daytime activity. As more does become receptive, buck movement can intensify, creating some of the season's most exciting opportunities.

For hunters, this is the time to stay alert, remain patient and make every sit count. A buck that has been moving mostly after dark may suddenly appear in daylight, following a doe through a hedgerow, crossing a field edge or slipping through a familiar patch of timber. Scrapes and rubs can offer clues to deer activity locations, but nothing compares with being in the woods when the rut is in full swing.

The timing of the rut varies from year to year and across individual areas, so there is no guaranteed peak day. Still, early to mid-November is traditionally a prime time period to watch for increased buck movement in Western New York.

According to experts, the rut is triggered by the photoperiod, like many things in nature. That is simply the ratio of daytime hours to nighttime hours. Experts say it is not affected by temperature or other weather factors, so say many experts. According to the onX app, the seeking phase of the rut started Halloween weekend and runs through Nov. 7, then chasing Nov. 8-12, then the peak rut Nov. 13-17. The post rut in Western New York will likely occur during the start of the firearm season, Nov. 18-28. Get out your calendars. On the other hand, you gotta go into the woods when you can. We all have different schedules and time in the woods is priceless. Just do go prepared with tick protection.

For archery hunters, the timing can be especially exciting. New York's Southern Zone early bowhunting season runs through Nov. 20, putting hunters in the woods during the best part of the rut. A well-timed encounter with a mature buck at close range is what keeps bowhunters returning season after season. With the wind in their favor, careful silent access to a stand and willingness to sit through changing conditions, hunters may find that their patience pays off.

St. George sought a special use permit to establish a concrete and asphalt recycling
local.body:
Pictured is the site of the proposed concrete and asphalt recycling yard owned and operated by Steve St. George.

OBSERVER Photos by Braden Carmen Steve St. George submitted plans for a concrete and asphalt recycling yard to be located at his operational property located in the town of Pomfret.

After three separate meetings with the Town of Pomfret Zoning Board of Appeals, Steve St. George was still without a permit for a concrete and asphalt recycling yard to be allowed at a property he owns in the town.

St. George sought a special use permit to establish a concrete and asphalt recycling yard at 3624 Webster Road, Fredonia. This property, formerly used for grape vineyards, is listed on the tax map as SBL:131.00-1-51.2. The property is zoned Agricultural/Residential (AR1).

St. George operates S. St. George Enterprises, a construction company that often works with roadways in the region. St. George is seeking a permit to recycle the materials from his company on site. St. George Enterprises operates six days a week, with Saturday hours limited 8 a.m. to noon. Operations are scaled back during the winter.

Initially, a building permit at the site was denied because the use was not defined under the zoning code's acceptable uses. That meant a special use permit was necessary for the project to proceed. The Zoning Board is required to evaluate the project under the State Environmental Quality Review Act guidelines.

Five members of the Board attended the recent meeting, with alternate Jonathan Townsend sitting in for Ruth Eckstrom. Code Enforcement Officer Warren Kelly was also in attendance.

After public opposition of the project in September from roughly a dozen guests, including seven members of the public that spoke on the matter, St. George sat alone in the audience at the latest meeting.

Gardner-Johnson on Tuesday, a day after he completed his one-game NFL suspension for spitting in the direction of Las Vegas Raiders players. The team did not provide any further details in announcing the move in a statement, though the le
local.body:
ORCHARD PARK -- The Buffalo Bills released veteran safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson on Tuesday, a day after he completed his one-game NFL suspension for spitting in the direction of Las Vegas Raiders players.

The team did not provide any further details in announcing the move in a statement, though the league discipline and Gardner-Johnson’s inconsistent performance were considered to play contributing factors.

Coach Joe Brady was non-committal regarding Gardner-Johnson’s status with the team when the NFL issued its suspension as the Bills entered their bye week off two weeks ago. And he sidestepped a question regarding the player on Monday, a day after Buffalo improved to 6-1 following a 36-10 win over Baltimore.

Brady would only say he had no discussions with Gardner-Johnson after the player returned to attend meetings. The NFL also granted the Bills a one-day exemption to carry an additional player through Tuesday.

The team is off until Thursday, when Buffalo resumes practice to prepare to play at Minnesota (6-1) on Monday night.

The 28-year-old signed a one-year contract with the Bills in March, with Buffalo becoming Gardner-Johnson’s sixth stop in five seasons, including two separate stints in Philadelphia. Though he won a Super Bowl with the 2024 Eagles, the eighth-year NFL player arrived in Buffalo with an established reputation of being a noted trash-talker and as someone who has on occasion crossed the line with illegal hits.

GM Brandon Beane acknowledged he consulted with coaches and had a lengthy discussion with Gardner-Johnson regarding his reputation before signing him.

Gardner-Johnson’s play was in question even before he was ejected for spitting during a post-whistle confrontation in a 33-30 win at Las Vegas on Oct. 18. He started six games at safety and was part of a secondary that was among the NFL’s worst against the pass.

local.body:
It’s been a confusing college football season so far. Nobody felt that more deeply than the College Football Playoff selection committee, which raised eyebrows aplenty in its first attempt of the season to make sense of it all.

Undefeated Miami received top billing in the committee’s opening crack at the CFP rankings Tuesday, followed by Georgia (7-1) and undefeated Utah.

From there, the 13 people in that room could have been picking from a hat. Defending champion Indiana (8-1) was ranked fourth -- eight spots ahead of Ohio State (6-2), which beat the Hoosiers 19-15 last month but has since lost quarterback Julian Sayin (to say nothing of another game).

At No. 5 was Alabama (6-2) -- eight spots ahead of Tennessee (6-2), even though the Tide is only a few weeks removed from a 16-point loss to the Vols. At No. 6 was Kentucky (7-1), followed by Texas (6-2).

UCLA, the nation’s only other undefeated team, was ranked eighth.

Oh, and Notre Dame. The Irish (7-1) were ranked 11th -- seven spots lower than their spot in the AP Top 25 -- and that ranking brought with it a simple message: As the last team that would make the bracket if the playoffs started today, they need to beat Miami on Saturday or risk slipping due to a schedule that clearly did not impress the committee.

“A very, very good football team,” committee chair Hunter Yurachek said of Notre Dame. “But when you look at Notre Dame’s schedule and the wins they have versus the teams ahead of them, they don’t have that signature win right now.”

In fact, Notre Dame’s biggest game so far resulted in its only loss -- 28-24 at BYU on Oct. 17.

local.summary: Voters return Cooney, Brouk, Ort and Helming in regional races.

Democrats took back the supermajority Tuesday in the New York state Senate and were poised for additional gains as final results roll in.

Locally, though, the balance of power stayed unchanged Tuesday, as incumbent Democratic Sens. Jeremy Cooney and Samra Brouk won re-election, as did Minority Leader Rob Ort and Republican Sen. Pam Helming.

local.summary: In Fairport, where one of the candidates waged a vigorous write in campaign, the mayoral race is too close to call.
local.body:
A vigorous write-in campaign for Fairport mayor left the race too close to call Tuesday night as unofficial vote tallies showed Democrat Heidi Woika trailing.

Woika, the village's deputy mayor, was the only name on the ballot. But she faced a challenge from Trustee Tracy Briggs, who lost the Democratic primary but continued to campaign. Write-ins accounted for 51% of the unofficial vote tally.

Those write-ins include but are not necessarily limited to Briggs. Next, a bipartisan team will review and tabulate those ballots to see where Briggs stands.

Elsewhere, Democrat Nick Coffee beat out incumbent Gates Supervisor Cosmo Giunta, a Republican, by a narrow margin. And in Chili, Republican Supervisor David Dunning led his opponent, Democrat Emily Kalouch by less than one point.

In the towns, a handful of supervisors who were elected last year had to run again this year due to a state law from 2023 that required town and county elections to shift from odd-numbered to even-numbered years.

The result: candidates elected last year to offices that otherwise had two-year terms served one-year terms that expire at the end of this year. That included many but not all town supervisors. In Greece, all town board seats were on the ballot.

local.title: Morelle re-elected. Here's what could await in the next Congress
local.summary: Voters returned Morelle to a fifth term and a possibly elevated national role focused on elections and anti-corruption measures.
local.body:
U.S. Rep. Joe Morelle was elected to a fifth term Tuesday, and will return to a Democratic majority in Congress.

"Now the hard work begins to restore trust for the American people that people in government are looking out for their interests," Morelle said. "And we're going to get to that work immediately."

Morelle defeated Republican challenger Virginia McIntyre, vastly outspending the Monroe County legislator and taking 62% of the vote in the Democrat-leaning district, according to unofficial tallies from the state Board of Elections. The district covers Monroe and extends into Ontario County.

In the nearby 24th District, which surrounds Monroe County, voters backed Republican Claudia Tenney's re-election bid by a slightly smaller margin over Democratic challenger Alissa Ellman.

Morelle's comments about next steps alluded to his expected role in the next Congress, championing a package of anti-corruption bills he helped to pen that could be the first legislation Democrats put forward. The Associated Press called the House majority for Democrats after 1 a.m. Wednesday, and called the Senate earlier in the night.

"If I'm blessed to have the chairmanship of the committee on House Administration, which looks tonight like that's likely, I'm going to work on putting an end to stock trading for members of Congress and people in the administration and the Supreme Court," the Irondequoit lawmaker said. "I'm going to put an end to people participating in the prediction markets. I'm going to put an end to dark money and make sure people are disclosing the influence of billionaires in our politics, and make sure that we reform campaign finance."

Morelle's campaign disbursements topped $2.1 million, including transfers to other candidate committees, and he had $468,000 cash on hand as of mid-October, according to federal campaign finance records . McIntyre's outlay was $66,000 — with her last financial disclosure showing her campaign nearly $11,000 in the red.

"I just would have liked it to have been tighter to really drive it home that you don't need that money and that power in order to run," McIntyre said. "You know, I think that we need fresh blood. We need fresh voices in there, and I want to make sure that they're not dissuaded from seeing the results tonight."

entertainment.title: ‘Dreams Do Come True’: Celebrities React as Democrats Sweep to Power In 2026 Midterm Election
entertainment.summary: Artists and actors everywhere joined the party, posting thoughts and outright joy on the historic Dems victory. And, for the Conservatives, a demoralizing defeat.
entertainment.body:
The political prognosticators warned of an incoming “blue wave.” As it turned out, the wave was more like a “blue tsunami” as the Democrats swept back into control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Explore Billboard Bruce Springsteen Mandy Moore See latest videos, charts and news

It was a long night for the Republicans, as the Senate slipped out of their grasp with the Democrats flipping Texas, Maine, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, and both Carolinas. Two dozen House seats flipped for the team in blue. Related The Lettermen's Tony Butala Dies at 87 Karol G Sweeps Latin Airplay's Top 3 With 'No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto' Tracks Steve Ellis, Love Affair Singer, Dies at 76

For the Democrats and their supporters around the globe, it was a night of celebration. And one that assures Donald Trump completes the final two years of his presidency as a “lame duck.”

Many artists and actors joined the party, posting thoughts and outright joy on the historic Dems victory. A return from power after years in the political wilderness. And, for the Conservatives, a demoralizing defeat.

Mandy Moore kept a close eye on the count, proof of which can be seen in here multiple posts on Instagram Stories . “Texas, this keeps getting better and better…” she writes. In another post, Moore acknowledges the work of Stacey Abrams, the politician, lawyer, and voting rights activist, who she described as as “a hero” who “opened the door for tonight.”

Henry Winkler is in his happy place. The veteran actor, who played the Fonz in “Happy Days,” responded to a post on X from social media Joanne Carducci, who put it out there: “Checking in — how are you all feeling right now?!!!” Winkler wrote, “Dreams do come true.”

Earlier, the likes of Olivia Rodrigo, Willie Nelson, Tinashe, and Bruce Springsteen urged their fellow Americans to get out and vote.

Adéla, like so many Europeans, was invested. Particularly so when, on the eve of Election Day, the White House TikTok shared a pro-Trump video using her hit song “Nicole Kidman” as the soundbed. The Slovak hit back with her own TikTok , pointing out to Trump and his supporters that the administration’s choice of song was “obviously so f—ing wrong, on so many levels. Because I stand for about zero of the things that that party stands for, and that person stands for.” Adéla couldn’t vote, but she suggested to those who can, do. Her “Go Vote” message was punctuated with a blue heart.

Announced at a special event at the National Film and Sound Archive of Australia in the nation’s capital, Canberra, 10 songs were elevated into The National Songbook, a new, annual initiative that recognizes the songs, songwriters and composers “whose creative vision has given voice to Australian stories.” Related The Lettermen's Tony Butala Dies at 87 Karol G Sweeps Latin Airplay's Top 3 With 'No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto' Tracks Steve Ellis, Love Affair Singer, Dies at 76

Among the standouts, Midnight Oil’s “Beds Are Burning,” the Easybeats’ “Friday On My Mind,” Helen Reddy’s “I Am Woman,” The Presets’ “My People,” Yothu Yindi’s “Treaty,” and Andrew “Banjo” Paterson’s “Waltzing Matilda.”

An initiative of APRA AMCOS and NFSA, the project preserves “the songs that have helped shape Australia’s cultural identity,” and launches to coincide with APRA’s 100th anniversary .

“No ten songs could ever tell the whole story of Australia, but together these inaugural inductees help us understand, as a nation, where we’ve come from, who we are and the values we’ve carried through generations,” comments Dean Ormston, CEO of APRA AMCOS.

“As APRA celebrates 100 years of championing songwriters, composers and music publishers, we welcome these debut entries into The National Songbook as songs that have helped become part of our shared cultural story, reflecting the extraordinary breadth, diversity and richness of Australian songwriting and composing.”

As it grows, the songbook will serve as a permanent digital archive, a vault that safeguards music treasures for future generations.

“The National Songbook reflects the remarkable breadth of Australian songwriting and composition, from songs of protest, belonging and identity to works that have become woven into our national story and our DNA,” remarks Meagan Loader, chief curator of the NFSA.

entertainment.title: Nithya Raman and Karen Bass Head to Costner ‘Swing Vote’ Territory
entertainment.summary: Wasn’t it only Florida that was supposed to be this dramatic?
entertainment.body:
They traded barbs for months and pillaged supporters by the barrel. So it was only fitting after all this that challenger Nithya Raman and incumbent Karen Bass would be deadlocked and separated by just a few thousand votes four hours after the polls closed in the L.A. mayor’s race. Hey, when you’ve got a good show going, you don’t cancel it mid-season. So Raman’s TV writer husband Vali Chandrasekaran could tell you. Or so anyone watching this race could tell you. As of midnight in Los Angeles some 4,000 votes separated Bass, in the lead, with Raman just behind her, with 600,000 votes counted. Given that there are 580,000 votes remaining, that lead tells us nothing. And given the fact that counting takes a long time — anything mail-in ballot postmarked today would still count in the next week — don’t expect a result anytime soon. Related Stories Midterms 2026 Trumper's Remorse: Voters Look at the Last Two Years, Ask for a Redo Midterms 2026 Kimmel Bashes Trump After Democrats' Midterms "Tsunami": "The Only Ass on His Mind Is the One That Just Got Handed to Him"

Raman and Bass are both Democrats , but Raman is to the left of Bass, if not as far to the left as her would-be New York counterpart Zohran Mamdani. Both Bass and Raman have pledged to do a lot for the film industry — but if you were running for mayor of Los Angeles right now, would you say anything else?

Still, this race isn’t the closest of the evening. That dubious honor goes to Scott Colom and Cindy Hyde-Smith vying for a Mississippi senate seat. With nearly a million votes in , Colom leads by…28 votes.

Raman has been here before, just last June in fact, when she initially trailed rival Spencer Pratt in the primary for the second spot behind Bass and then slowly clawed her way back to finally take the spot a week later. Bass has been here before too. Her race was similarly tight with Rick Caruso four years ago, and she would go on to win by nearly ten points. It took three weeks. Get ready for a lot of post-credit scenes.

This is part of The Hollywood Reporter’s ongoing midterm coverage. You can check out all of our pieces here .

entertainment.title: Trumper’s Remorse: Voters Look at the Last Two Years and Ask for a Redo
entertainment.summary: With a crushing Democratic rout in both the House and Senate, America seems to want to Replayola everything that's happened since 2024.
entertainment.body: Even the most forgiving retailers tend to cap a return policy at 90 days. Show up after that, you’re out of luck. But voters across America on Tuesday took a look at what they purchased two Novembers ago and said: “How about 730 days, would you accept that? The merchandise is a little battered, but the tags are intact.” After months of political fighting both substantive and surreal, with debates over ideology and reflections on buttocks, American voters Tuesday delivered as strong a rebuff to a Republican president as has been delivered in four decades, turning the House of Representatives and Senate over to Democrats and essentially saying “you see if you can stop him.” Democrats won in swing states and they won in red states; they won in states where Trump had been ascendant and states where Republicans never gave up control. They won with moderates and they won with firebrands. They won, improbably, in rural counties all over the country. From Maine to Texas, Kansas to South Carolina — heck, as of this writing even Mississippi was in play — new Democratic Senators were springing up everywhere. They won so often cable news pundits ran out of water puns for their blue-wave metaphor. They won so much, they may have even gotten tired of winning. Democrats gained, as of this writing, a whopping 41 seats in the House, far more than the three needed to win control. But it was the Senate — where a flip was far from assured and in fact unlikely just weeks ago — where the most drama abided. The four-seat requirement was met. Then it became five. Then six. States where Democrats hadn’t won a Senate seat in 38 years ( Texas ) or in 94 years (Kansas). States where Trump two years ago won by double digits (Ohio) and states where Strom Thurmond presided for half a century (South Carolina). And even, it turned out, in a state where Democrats hadn’t beaten a Susan Collins in 30 years (Maine). As of this writing, Democrats had flipped seven Senate seats with an eye on an eighth in Alaska and a ninth in Mississippi, using every last vote of that 43-vote lead . They were also holding on to all their blue seats, including Michigan, called by CNN for Abdul El-Sayed at 2:30 am local time. There have been major Congressional shifts like his before, most notably in 1994 for Republicans and 2008 for Democrats. But both of those quakes occurred because of a galvanizing candidate in the winning party — Newt Gingrich in 1994 and Barack Obama in 2008. What was remarkable about this sweep is that it didn’t come from one central charismatic figure but a slew of grassroots personalities who understood their individual constituencies, state-by-state: James Talarico and Josh Turek and Annie Andrews and Adam Hamilton. (Also, speaking of Talarico and Hamilton, it’s nice Democrats finally figured out what the Republicans did decades ago: overtly Christian candidates play.) And, of course, the Trump remorse. Because there was a political figure who mobilized the electorate — just in the negative. How fittingly 2026 that the candidate who influenced voters most was the one people liked least, Donald Trump , with his policies on ICE and Iran, with his DOGE slashings and science evisceratings and health-care-benefit reducing and the fact that prices still seem to be going up while the only thing that seems to be coming down is the East Wing. “American people are hurting,” Van Jones said on CNN, boiling it to the quick, “and this dude’s out of touch.” Perhaps the best modern comp to all this is 1986. That Election Day, 40 years ago, Democrats scored big in the midterms — also in the second term of a fading Republican giant, netting eight seats during the presidency of Ronald Reagan. This election season has been one of the most entertaining, if also the most divisive, in recent memory as a showman president distrusted even by many of his own party paved the way to a series of colorful and ultimately losing showdowns. Books can be written about all the dynamics, but fights over Middle East policy of course roiled and at times threatened to break apart the Democratic party — right up until the final days with Haley Stevens’ shocking defection in Michigan. And yet somehow it all led to history — the first openly gay male senator in New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas , the first Black female governor in Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms. Meanwhile, Republicans tried to look toward the future while grappling with the Donald Trump present, accepting his campaign appearances even as they kept him out of nearly all of their ads. (Democrats, on the other hand, were all too happy to tether their opponents to the president.) And through it all the president himself, getting distracted with boasts and random talk as he hit the hustings of a trail where he was only ambivalently wanted. The Democrats will face mountains ahead, not least thanks to the schisms in their own party; how will the Darializa Chevalier and Melat Kiros types in the House play with the mainstream types led by new speaker Hakeem Jeffries (the first Black Speaker in American history). And, in the Senate, how will Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed meld with moderates like Turek and Hamilton, not to mention Majority Leader Chuck Schumer. The Democrats will also have to decide how much to lean into inquiries and investigations, as this is not what voters sent them to Washington for — it’s the economy, stupid, as James Carville’s whiteboard words continue to redound. But the bigger questions lie with Republicans, who now must decide in the minority how to oppose Democrats — how much to genuflect to a man they have spent much of the past decade paying fealty to, now newly irrelevant. Perhaps the person most confused today, strategically: JD Vance. What or whom exactly is he supposed to be defending, and how does he find a path to the 2028 primaries intact? entertainment.title: Australian Consumer Advocacy Group Blasts Ticketing Giants for ‘Fleecing Fans’
entertainment.summary: Reps for Ticketmaster and Ticketek have responded.
entertainment.body:
Ticketek and Ticketmaster have collected Choice’s Shonky Awards, a dubious honor handed out to those businesses deemed to offer some of the nation’s worst products and services.

The ticketing giants were responsible for “fleecing fans,” remarks Choice CEO Monique Perry , as the consumer advocacy group on Wednesday (Nov. 4) announced its 2026 Shonkys. Related Kenny MacPherson, Veteran Music Publisher and Big Deal Music Co-Founder, Dies at 71 Jessica Lynch

The ticketing companies were fingered for “gouging consumers during a cost-of-living crisis,” reads a statement issued by Choice. “Both companies have used a number of sneaky tactics, like dynamic pricing or ‘in demand’ tickets, to push ticket prices for live events to ridiculous new heights.”

Time and time again, Perry continues, the ticketing companies have used “sneaky tactics such as dynamic pricing or higher-cost ‘in demand’ tickets, concealing ticket prices ahead of sale and strict time limits to take advantage of fans desperately wanting to secure a spot. We think that’s pretty shonky.”

In one example provided by the not-for-profit organization, John Farnham fans who logged on to Ticketek to secure tickets to a tribute concert were faced with inflated prices of up to A$1,650 ($1,153).

“Ticketmaster is committed to giving fans a safe, secure and transparent way to buy tickets to thousands of events each year. We continually invest in technology to protect fans, improve the ticket-buying experience, and make ticketing more transparent across our platform,” reads a statement issued to Billboard from the ticketing giant, part of Live Nation. Ticket prices are set by event organizers, not Ticketmaster, the message continues. “We do not use surge pricing or algorithms that automatically increase prices in response to real-time demand.”

And for “in demand tickets,” event organizers set the prices of hot tickets “closer to market value and may review these over the sales period. These prices do not automatically increase because more fans join a queue,” the Ticketmaster statement reads.

“We’re committed to helping fans understand how ticketing works and providing clear information about ticket pricing and their options.”

entertainment.title: CISAC Reports Record Global Creator Royalties, Warns of ‘Largest Test’ From AI
entertainment.summary: Digital is now the largest generator of publishing royalties, accounting for 45.6% of the total.
entertainment.body:
Global music publishing collections grew to nearly 14.6 billion euros ($15.89 billion) in 2025, up 11.9% from the prior year’s total of 12.6 billion euros ($13.62 billion), according to data published in CISAC’s latest Global Collections Report.

CISAC director general Gadi Oron noted that the growth demonstrates “both the resilience of collective management and the enduring demand for creative works around the world.” Related Kenny MacPherson, Veteran Music Publisher and Big Deal Music Co-Founder, Dies at 71 Jessica Lynch

However, more than half of the increase, or 6.6 percentage points was due to the first time inclusion of revenue from the Mechanical Licensing Collective (MLC), the U.S. collection agency, while only only about 5.3 percentage points came from organic growth. On the other hand, the 5.3% organic growth from publishing outpaced the 4.8% increase for 2025, as counted by IFPI, that the record label side of the music business experienced.

While the industry is still growing, a counterbalance worry is how the double-edged sword of artificial intelligence will impact the economic model.

“Our confederation now faces its largest test with artificial intelligence, new business models and changing patterns of consumption,” Oron writes in the forward to the CISAC annual report. “This technological change also means that the future can bring real opportunities for creators…The issue is no longer whether AI will transform our industries, but whether the systems that protect creators’ rights are evolving quickly enough to keep pace.”

Fortunately, CISAC and its member societies are at the center of the debate around new laws, and is “contributing to numerous consultations, policy debates and legislative processes around the world, so as to ensure that creators’ rights remain at the heart of AI policy making,” Oron wrote.

Adds CISAC president and ABBA co-founder Björn Ulvaeus , “Human creativity is not something to be replaced or bypassed. It is something to be valued, protected and celebrated. And I hope that if we get it right, artificial intelligence will not diminish human creativity but will help inspire its next chapter.”

Getting back to the numbers, digital is now the largest generator of publishing royalties comprising 45.6% of music publishing royalties. In 2025, digital royalties totaled 6.41 billion euros ($7.25 billion) or a 28% increase over the 5.01 billion euros ($5.42 billion) collected in 2024. But it is here where the additional of the MLC is having its biggest impact.

Logo text Jimmy Kimmel became the first late night host to take on the results of the 2026 midterm elections late Tuesday night.

While none of the major late night shows went live on election night, ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel Live! reportedly taped later than usual on Tuesday night to react to some of the early returns. Comedy Central’s The Daily Show was the only other major late night show to air a new episode Tuesday night, but that was taped before many of the polls closed. Stephen Colbert regularly took his Late Show live on election nights, but, of course, CBS canceled his show last year and it came to an end in May. Kimmel’s late taping allowed the host to get in some early jokes on a night that saw the Democrats projected to win both the House and the Senate amid historic, surprise victories in Georgia, Texas , Ohio, South Carolina and Kansas.

entertainment.title: Ben Shapiro Says 2026 Midterms Were “A Wipeout for Republicans”: “The President Was Kind of on the Ballot”
entertainment.summary: The conservative commentator noted Tuesday night, before most of the major race results were called, that "this not an evening to remember."
entertainment.body:
Ben Shapiro reacted to the early results of the 2026 midterms during an appearance on the All-In podcast Tuesday night, noting that he thinks early tallies indicated that “the president was kind of on the ballot.”

“This not an evening to remember,” he said on the podcast, which streamed from 8 p.m. ET to 10 p.m. ET on Tuesday night, before some of the major race results were called. “I think that, honestly, the president said going in that the election was going to be a referendum on him, act like he’s on the ballot, and I think that, you know, the president was kind of on the ballot.” Related Stories Midterms 2026 Xavier Becerra Defeats Steve Hilton to Become California's First Latino Governor in 150 Years Midterms 2026 Texas Turns Blue: How James Talarico, Gina Hinojosa Broke Dems' 36-Year Losing Streak

Shapiro argued “if this were just the case of a few outstandingly bad Republican candidates losing, like Paxton in Texas, for example, or if it were just a matter of an outstanding Democrat candidate winning somewhere, like Josh Turek in Iowa, … but the fact that South Carolina is going, you basically have an empty suit in South Carolina losing.”

Texas had history-making results , as the state elected James Talarico as defeated Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat elected as a senator in 38 years; Gina Hinojosa also beat Greg Abbott to become the first Democratic governor of Texas in 36 years.

As for South Carolina, Annie Andrews became the state’s first Democrat elected to the Senate in over 20 years. She also became the first woman from South Carolina to be elected to the Senate.

“Or the fact that Florida stayed red, but very, very, very closely. I mean, that’s my home state so I know that state very well, Angie Nixon is a full-scale nutcase, and Angie Nixon is going to lose that senatorial race by about two points,” he added. (Democrat Nixon was defeated by Republican Ashley Moody in Florida’s U.S. Senator race.)

“It’s a wipeout for Republicans,” Shapiro asserted. “There’s no way to sugarcoat that. And again, if you’re looking at it across the map, that bodes pretty ill for 2028.”

entertainment.title: Hasan Piker Threatens Further Legal Action Against Conservative Pundits He Claims Have Defamed Him
entertainment.summary: The Twitch streamer's legal team recently filed a $72.5 million defamation lawsuit against CNN contributor Scott Jennings.
entertainment.body:
After filing a $72.5 million defamation lawsuit against CNN contributor Scott Jennings last week, the progressive political Twitch streamer Hasan Piker ‘s legal team is promising more legal action against conservative pundits they feel have defamed their client.

In an interview with Vanity Fair , Piker’s attorney and defamation specialist Daniel Watkins said there is a “reckoning coming.” “There are other people and other entities that will likely receive outreach from my law firm in the coming days,” Watkins said.

The more aggressive legal posture from Piker’s camp stands in marked contrast to his previous tendency to let the more controversial, and often baseless, accusations against him slide. Since he became a national and international political figure — he has been namechecked by both Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu in 2026 — Piker has faced a torrent of claims against him, including animal abuse, racism and misogyny, and has become something of a lightning rod for Republican and centrist Democratic attacks. Related Stories Business Hasan Piker Files $72.5 Million Defamation Lawsuit Against Scott Jennings Over Lynching Quote General News Wild! Mattel Sets UNO Card-Game Competition Series to Stream on Twitch

That all changed on Aug. 11, when Jennings, appearing on his Salem Media podcast, presented a spliced video montage alleging that Piker advocated for lynchings. Jennings used the completely out-of-context segment to urge Michigan voters to reject Senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed over his ties to the streamer.

Watkins issued a formal retraction demand to Salem Media’s chief legal counsel, Christopher Henderson, in late August. When that yielded no response, Piker filed suit, demanding $27.5 million in compensatory damages and $45 million in punitive damages.

“I have been very deliberately anti-litigation for a very long time,” Piker told Vanity Fair . “But something shifted that’s been bubbling up where… people like Scott Jennings , and there are others as well, started trafficking in outright lies, defamation, and slander.”

Watkins stressed the severe impact of the clips on Piker’s career, calling the targeted misattributions “disgusting and vile and dangerous” for a public figure built on advocacy for marginalized groups. entertainment.title: Xavier Becerra Defeats Steve Hilton to Become California’s First Latino Governor in 150 Years
entertainment.summary: The former attorney general cruised to victory. But now he has his work cut out for him.
entertainment.body:
Democrat Xavier Becerra will be the next California governor, according to the Associated Press, defeating Republican Steve Hilton to become the state’s first Latino governor in more than 150 years.

The AP called the race just after the polls closed in the Golden State at 8 p.m. on Tuesday. As of 9:30 p.m., with 49 percent of ballots counted, Becerra had a substantial lead over Hilton.

“What a great night to be a Californian. What a great night to be an American,” Becerra said in his victory speech. “To be the son of immigrants from a union household to be standing in victory with all of you. Now, I’m not gonna sugarcoat it. These past two years have been tough: higher prices, more wars, corruption and lawlessness. But we hung in there; fought back. It felt like Mission: Impossible . We knew it was mission necessary.” Related Stories Midterms 2026 Chris Pappas Becomes First Openly Gay Man Elected to Senate Midterms 2026 Kathy Hochul's Win in New York Assures a Hollywood Home for Years to Come

He added, “And tonight, sisters and brothers, because of your tireless work, we can proudly utter the inspiring battle cry of our beloved and departed sister and warrior Dolores Huerta: ‘Sí, se puede.’ Yes, we can! Yes, we did! We fought and we won!”

Heading into election night, the odds were already against Britain-born Hilton, as California hasn’t elected a Republican to any statewide office in two decades. The last Republican to lead the Golden State was Arnold Schwarzenegger, whose term ended in 2011.

Given that registered Democrats outnumber Republicans by 4.6 million voters in the state, any Republican starts at a disadvantage. For Hilton specifically, receiving an endorsement from Donald Trump also likely didn’t help, as the Republican president is widely loathed outside his conservative base in a state he often criticizes (Most recently, Trump was slammed in October for suggesting Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if it were allowed to develop a nuclear weapon.)

In attempts to win over California voters, Hilton, a former Fox News host, also leveraged his media-savvy background with some headline-making campaign ads, specifically his “Just Try It, California” ad that featured two young women making sexual innuendos and his viral “Barstow street taco” blunder from his video outside the original Del Taco location.

When it came to policies, while Hilton focused his campaign on targeting government waste, high living costs, education reform and public safety — such as wanting to eliminate state income tax on the first $150,000 earned by residents, lower gas prices to $3 per gallon, implement statewide homeless encampment bans and propose a film tax credit as high as 60 percent to save Hollywood — it ultimately wasn’t enough to overcome Becerra.

entertainment.title: Texas Turns Blue: How James Talarico, Gina Hinojosa Broke Dems’ 36-Year Losing Streak
entertainment.summary: Why Talarico and Hinojosa managed to flip both Texas’ U.S. Senate seat and governor’s mansion.
entertainment.body:
For the first time in 38 years, a Democrat has been elected senator in Texas.

And for the first time in 36 years, a Democrat has been elected governor of Texas.

Riding a blue wave of anti-Trump sentiment, James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton in the traditional red state, fulfilling a decades-long dream come true for Democrats, while Gina Hinojosa beat Greg Abbott to take the governor’s mansion.

“David wasn’t as big or as strong as Goliath but he had hope, he had faith and he had a slingshot.” Talarico told supporters at around 11:30 pm local time. “You were my slingshot.” Related Stories Midterms 2026 Chris Pappas Becomes First Openly Gay Man Elected to Senate Midterms 2026 Kathy Hochul's Win in New York Assures a Hollywood Home for Years to Come

With final election results still coming in, both NBC and CNN called the race for Talarico. About 85 percent of the votes have been tallied as of late Tuesday night, and Talarico is up some 12 points. With the same count in, Hinojosa is up seven points, and CNN and NBC have now called that contest too.

The candidates’ performance was the result of a perfect storm of circumstances (as CNN’s Alyssa Farah Griffin said early in the evening, “If Texas were ever going to go blue, it’s now”).

There was, clearly, some of the strongest tailwinds for Democrats in years given widespread dissatisfaction with President Trump, who currently has some of the worst poll numbers of his political career.

There were the candidates themselves. Talarico is an unabashed Christian, telegenic and charismatic, making himself rather hard to dislike — even as the GOP spent an estimated $221 million on negative attack ads to brand him as a progressive radical. While Hinojosa ran a populist campaign focused on lowering household costs, raising teacher pay and challenging corporate influence in state government.

Barbie released its first-ever Diwali doll in 2024 in collaboration with Indian fashion designer Anita Dongre, and the limited-edition collectible quickly sold out in stores and online. The Barbie Diwali doll commemorates the annual celebration popular in Indian culture and known worldwide as the “Festival of Lights” (the word Diwali means “ row of lights ” in Hindi). Barbie’s Diwali doll is dressed in a festive, Moonlight Bloom set with a choli top, floral Koti vest and lehenga skirt adorned with dahlias, jasmine and Indian lotus symbolizing strength and beauty, according to a press release sent to Billboard . The doll accessorizes with golden bangles and shimmering earrings.
